abstract: Summary The plant community has a strong track record of RNA sequencing technology deployment, which combined with the recent advent of spatial platforms (e.g. 10× genomics) has resulted in an explosion of single‐cell and nuclei datasets that can be positioned in an in situ context within tissues (e.g. a cell atlas). In the genomics era, application of proteomics technologies in the plant sciences has always trailed behind that of RNA sequencing technologies, largely due in part to upfront cost, ease‐of‐use, and access to expertise. Conversely, the use of early analytical tools for characterizing small molecules (metabolites) from plant systems predates nucleic acid sequencing and proteomics analysis, as the search for plant‐based natural products has played a significant role in improving human health throughout history. As the plant sciences field now aims to fully define cell states, cell‐specific regulatory networks, metabolic asymmetry and phenotypes, the measurement of proteins and metabolites at the single‐cell level will be paramount. As a result of these efforts, the plant community will unlock exciting opportunities to accelerate discovery and drive toward meaningful translational outcomes.
body:
Introduction
The plant community has a strong track record of RNA sequencing technology deployment, which combined with the recent advent of spatial platforms (e.g. 10× genomics) has resulted in an explosion of single‐cell and nuclei datasets that can be positioned in an
in situ
context within tissues (e.g. a cell atlas) (Han
et al
.,
2023
; Liu
et al
.,
2023
; Serrano
et al
.,
2024
). In the genomics era, application of proteomics technologies in the plant sciences has always trailed behind that of RNA sequencing technologies, largely due in part to upfront costs (instrumentation is relatively expensive), ease‐of‐use, and access to expertise. Conversely, the use of early analytical tools for characterizing small molecules (metabolites) from plant systems predates nucleic acid sequencing and proteomics analysis, as the search for plant‐based natural products has played a significant role in improving human health throughout history (Biemann,
2002
). However, the development and application of approaches to measure metabolites within single cells or spatially across tissues in plants has found limited traction.
As the plant sciences field now aims to fully define cell states and phenotypes, the measurement of proteins and metabolites, in conjunction with transcripts, at the single‐cell level will be paramount to succeeding in these efforts (Zeng,
2022
). Pursuit of measuring these biomolecules in single plant cells renders a need for rapid and precise measurements, as well as the deployment of highly sensitive and reproducible proteomics and metabolomics assays. A brief literature search of the application of these single‐cell omics technologies in mammalian research will reveal a recent surge in innovation and translational discoveries. As such, the plant community has an opportunity to retool these methods and approaches to make them suitable for analyzing plant systems. This means that while plant scientists may be lagging behind their peers researching mammalian systems, the silver lining is that our community can capitalize on their efforts and have an opportunity to quickly and effectively develop single‐cell approaches for this new research landscape in plant sciences. A recent successful example of this was illustrated by Montes
et al
., where they demonstrated the power of single‐cell proteomics to resolve cellular heterogeneity within Arabidopsis roots and differentiate expression of nearly 600 proteins indicative of plant cell types (Montes
et al
.,
2024
).
Where we stand
Over the past 15 years, the fields of proteomics and metabolomics have benefited from the rapid advancement of mass spectrometry (MS) instrumentation, placing us on the precipice of being able to readily deploy these tools for single‐cell biology in plants (Fig.
1
). The use of time‐of‐flight (TOF) and magnetic sector mass analyzers led to quadrupoles then trapping instruments and Fourier‐transform‐based MS capabilities, which have now culminated to advanced TOF‐instruments (including asymmetric track lossless MS systems), which promise a bright future for cell‐type, single cell, and perhaps even single nuclei omics in plants due to their exceptional sensitivity. The speed at which these instruments can acquire data (15 min vs 2 h for the same depth of analyses) means more samples analyzed faster, driving per sample cost reductions and increased accessibility to quantitative proteomics and metabolomics. Also promising is that MS instrument vendors have begun to focus on cutting the cost of these instruments toward the price of high‐resolution optical microscopy systems, driving the total cost of performing these assays toward sub‐$1000 USD per sample, including total cost of instrument ownership. In comparison, commercially available spatial transcriptomics assays typically cost > 4× per sample, mainly due to reagent cost. Note, none of these cost include bioinformatics support or expertise.
Fig. 1
New approaches for
ex situ
and
in situ
single‐cell mass spectrometry (MS)‐based proteomics and metabolomics are being developed for plant biology. Here, cells can be extracted, protoplasted, and sorted for deep targeted and untargeted proteomics and/or metabolomics. For protein analysis, this is typically performed in a bottom‐up approach, where proteins are enzymatically digested, the resulting peptides are then analyzed, and detection of said peptide(s) encodes for detection of a respective protein. Alternatively,
in situ
methods using MS imaging can measure metabolites and proteins directly from tissue‐embedded cells. Either of these approaches can be integrated with transcriptomics data to provide a holistic systems biology understanding of cell phenotypes and states.
Beyond standard bottom‐up chromatography‐based MS methods, developments in MS imaging (MSI) instrumentation also offer promising new opportunities for cost‐effectively accelerating single‐cell and cell‐type analyses in plants. Here, the use of sophisticated laser optic configurations for matrix‐assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI) approaches can provide
in situ
spatial metabolomics measurements of single cells directly from plant tissue, for example (Korte
et al
.,
2015
; Dueñas
et al
.,
2018
; Taylor
et al
.,
2021
). Particularly, MSI‐based spatial metabolomics has the unique opportunity to provide deeper insights into the synthesis and regulatory mechanisms underlying growth, development, and response to (a)biotic stress(es) of tissue‐embedded plant cells (Yin
et al
.,
2023
).
To date, the plant community has lagged behind the pioneering protein‐ and metabolite‐based single‐cell and cell‐type research of other fields (e.g. mammalian and clinical research). The sample processing and data analysis approaches associated with these developments was recently reviewed and contextualized for the plant community (Clark
et al
.,
2022
). Only a handful of cell‐type proteomics and metabolomics studies in plant systems have emerged, indicating that while technical barriers persist in readily generating MS‐based single‐cell omics data from plants, these barriers can be overcome. Of the existing proteomics‐focused publications, most have utilized a cell‐type approach focused on photosynthetic tissues (Huebbers
et al
.,
2023
; Wang
et al
.,
2023
), with only a single published paper to date related to root tissue analysis (Montes
et al
.,
2024
). Interestingly, this contrasts with the plant scRNAseq and snRNAseq research, where roots represent the model organ and where the most reliable cell markers currently exist across diverse plant genetics. Provided as such, this makes roots arguably the best opportunity for further development and benchmarking single‐cell proteomics and metabolomics assay approaches.
The promise of plant cell‐type data and integration
Integration of diverse cell‐type data (e.g. ‘multi‐omic’) is an emerging frontier in human research. Here, new multi‐omic approaches developed on mammalian tissues, like the RNA sequencing‐based and/or protein‐metabolite‐based assays that can be performed on the same cells, illuminate the bright future for the integration of diverse cell‐type data from plant tissues (Mezger
et al
.,
2021
; James
et al
.,
2022
). In plants, the goal of generating cell‐type data is grounded in our ability to better refine where and when cellular processes take place, and then to ultimately integrate this data across modalities to form new hypotheses centering on rational biotechnology development and/or plant breeding (Cole
et al
.,
2021
; Plant Cell Atlas Consortium
et al
.,
2021
). This is particularly important when looking to define the ‘ground truth’ cell states, cell‐specific regulatory networks and metabolic asymmetry (Veličković
et al
.,
2018
), which have previously gone undetected in bulk analyses, but offer a new frontier in precision agriculture. It is here that MS‐based technologies offer substantive advantages. While perhaps not yet generating the data depth of scRNA‐seq or snRNA‐seq, MS‐centric analyses can offer critical insight into changing protein abundances, metabolic landscapes, and post‐translational regulation events in ways that compliment genomic technologies. Integration of these multi‐omic data through computational modeling will together unravel what defines the ‘ground truth’ of a cell phenotype and state.
Immediate challenges for single‐cell proteomics and metabolomics
Beyond just adapting the technological, workflow, and bioinformatics advancements pioneered using nonphotosynthetic eukaryotic systems, we must consider that multicellular photosynthetic eukaryotes have a number of challenges that require the development of standardized workflows. These include the following: the need to
de novo
derive cell populations from intact plant tissues, which has already been accomplished in mammalian disease research—recent use of new microdissection tools provide an alternative means by which single plant cells can be rapidly isolated for analysis (Balasubramanian
et al
.,
2021
); the presence of a cell wall in plants that requires digestion to generate protoplasts for analysis—doing this can not only result in mixed populations of cells but also result in artefactual findings from the process of digesting the cell wall. Indeed, we cannot understate the broad importance of how new sample preparation and handling methods will be needed for single‐cell analyses in plants, as the approaches developed in the mammalian research fields may not necessarily directly translate. Worth noting is that much of the ability to do single cell analyses, as highlighted for example by the recent paper from Montes
et al
. (
2024
), was enabled by advancements in sample preparation and handling, and not just by new instrument technology. Many of these approaches and technologies are in their infancy for plant sciences, and they often require highly trained expertise. In reality, more development will be needed to make them broadly utilizable across plant science‐focused laboratories.
Nevertheless, with the per sample costs of single‐cell proteomics on a trajectory to decrease with faster MS instrumentation, it will be possible to create repositories of the ‘non‐specific PROTOPLASTome’ across different tissues and cell types to enhance quality controls and cell‐type proteome precision, similar to initiatives such as the ‘CRAPome’ (Mellacheruvu
et al
.,
2013
). Further, with increased community investment, enhanced optimization and standardization of protoplast generation procedures across diverse plant models, tissues, and organs will enable the production of quantitative, cell‐type protein‐metabolite‐based data that are comparable across studies and systems. In doing this, the plant community will unlock exciting opportunities to accelerate its discovery potential and drive toward translational outcomes.
